grammarNotes: In this lesson, you’ll learn the 10 Commandments in English.
God gave Moses the 10 Commandments in a tablet at Mount Sinai. That story is in Exodus 20.
Before you read the 10 Commandments, can you remember them in Portuguese. Take your time and think about it.
Now here they are in English. How many can you remember?
Have no other God but me.
Do not make an idol of anything in heaven or on earth or under the earth. Do not bow down to them or worship them.
Do not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.
Observe the Sabbath and keep it holy.
5. Honor your father and your mother.
6. Do not murder.
7. Do not commit adultery.
8. Do not steal.
9. Do not give false testimony.
10. Do not covet your neighbor’s house.
From: The Good News Bible, Exodus 20
Guess where the verbs in each commandment are. For example, 1 Have
Pause the video and write down the verbs. In some commandments, there are 2 or 3 verbs.
And the answers are:
Have
Take
Observe
Honor
Murder
Commit
Steal
Give
Covet
The verbs in the 10 Commandments are
a. in the simple present
b. in the imperative
If you guessed “b. the imperative”, you’re right. This form of the verb is good for commands (orders) or Instructions.
Now, look at the verbs. Which are affirmative? Which are negative?
Negative – do not make – do not bow down – do not worship – do not murder – do not commit – do not steal – do not give – do not covet
As you can see, you form the imperative with the infinitive (e.g., to do, that is, the name of the verb)
a. with TO
b. without TO
The answer is b. WITHOUT to
You form the imperative with the infinitive form of the verb without TO.
In the negative, add DO NOT before the verb.
In informal situations and in speaking, use the contraction “Don’t”.
The imperative is always in the second person.
(You) Honor your father and your mother.
When the imperative involves the First person I or we, you use LET US + verb.
Informally and in speaking, use the contraction Let’s (Let us).
Let us go (you and me).
Let´s go.
It’s polite to use PLEASE with imperatives.
Now please do more exercises about the imperative form on the platform and let’s practice this more!

grammarNotes: Let’s learn more verbs. Let’s learn about ACTION VERBS. These verbs describe actions, for example:
SING, PRAY, RUN, DRIVE A CAR, RIDE A BIKE, READ, SLEEP, TALK, DANCE, STAND UP, SIT DOWN, KNEEL DOWN

Let’s practice this vocabulary about action verbs and the imperative form. Let’s play a game! The name of the game is “Simon says”. Literalmente em português Simon says quer dizer “O Simon disse”, ou seja, deu uma ordem. Tem um jogo semelhante que chamamos de “O Rei mandou”. Como Jesus é o nosso Rei, vamos mudar o nome do jogo para “Jesus says”. When I say, “Jesus says, “Stand up”, you stand up! When I say, “Dance”, you dance. Do you understand?
Let’s see an example with Dudu and Samuel.

Jesus says, “Stand up”. Jesus says, “Dance”. Jesus says, “Drive a car”. Jesus says, “Run”. Jesus says, “Ride a bike”.  Jesus says, “Talk”. Jesus says, “Sing”. Jesus says, “Sleep”. Jesus says, “Kneel down”. Jesus says, “Pray”. Very good”!
Assista ao vídeo novamente e tire o som. Write the action verbs. Then listen again with the sound and check your answers.
The answers are: STAND UP, DANCE, DRIVE A CAR, RUN, RIDE A BIKE, TALK, SING, SLEEP, KNEEL DOWN, PRAY

grammarNotes: In this lesson, you’ll learn about vowels before nasals.

Em português, temos vogais nasais, ou seja, na pronúncia o ar sai pelo nariz an (manga), en (ontem), in (sim), on (ontem), un (mundo). Em inglês não há essas vogais. Todas são orais, ou seja, o ar sai pela boca. Então, há uma tendência entre nós falantes de português de nasalizar as vogais que vem antes de sons nasais em inglês, que são 3: n, m  e ng, representados pelas letras n, m e ng. Devemos tentar evitar essa tendência.
For example, in the prepositions of place, the pronunciation is /in/, /an/, /un/. Also, pronounce the n after the vowel /in/.
Listen and repeat. Pronounce the vowel and then the letter n.

grammarNotes: In this lesson, we’ll learn about locations in a town or a city. Let’s use the vocabulary from the places in a city from the previous video.
Look at the picture of locations.
Note that you use the verb to be to express locations. It’s equivalent to SEE ou FICAR in Portuguese.
A loja é na rua A. = A loja fica na rua A.
The house is on First Street.
Note que para endereços, ao contrário do português, o nome da rua vem primeiro e depois a palavra que indica se é uma rua, avenida, etc.
You use the preposition on when it is just the name of the street or avenue, etc.
The house is on First Street.
You use the preposition at when there is the number and the name of the street or avenue, etc.
The house is at 5 First Street.
The hotel is near the bank.
O hotel fica perto do banco.
The church is on the corner of First and Second Street.
A igreja fica na esquina da rua A com a B.
The mall is across from / in front of the school.
Tem duas expressões para em frente a: across from é quando tem algo no meio, por exemplo, uma rua, um rio; in front of é quando é simplesmente em frente.
The restaurant is next to the shop. The restaurant is on the right. The shop is on the left.
A loja fica (ou é) ao lado, vizinho ao restaurante.
To ask about locations, ou seja, para perguntar onde fica um lugar, the question is:
Where’s the church?
It’s on the corner of First and Second Street.

grammarNotes: In this lesson, we’ll talk about directions. But first, let’s talk about the apostle Paul. Do you remember his conversion? Think about it.
Now read the passage about Paul’s conversion and answer the questions.
Jesus: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?
Saul: Who are you? Lord?
Jesus: I am Jesus, whom you persecute. Now get up and go to the city.
Saul: I’m blind. Take me to the city.
In Damascus, Jesus calls Ananias, his disciple, in a vision.
Jesus: Ananias, go to the house of Judas, on Straight Street. Pray for a man named Saul from Tarsus.
Ananias goes to Judas’ house. He prays for Saul and he can see again.
Saul: I can see again!! Thank God!
1. Paul’s conversion was on the way to:
a. Jerusalem		b. Damascus		c. Bethlehem
2. On the way, Paul sees:
a. the sun		b. a light		c. the moon		in heaven.
3. God changes his name, but Paul’s previous name is:
a. Saul			b. Simon		c. Tarsus
And the answers are:
B	2. B	3. A
In this passage in the Bible, Jesus gives directions to two people – Paul (or Saul) and Ananias.
Directions are instructions for people to go to a certain place. Read the text again and find the two directions.
And the answers are:
a. Get up and go to the city.
b. Go to the house of Judas, on Straight Street.
To give directions, you also use the imperative form.
Go to Straight Street.
Today we have GPS in our cell phones, but it is important to understand the directions they give.
A common question for directions is
How do I get to the Tower of David?
Where’s the Tower of David?
Here are some common expressions for directions.
Listen to the directions. Follow them on the map.
You are a tourist in Jerusalem. You’re at the King David Hotel on King David Street. You want to go to the Tower of David Museum. Look at the directions in the dialogue below.

grammarNotes: In this lesson, you’ll read about Jesus’ final instructions to his disciples. That is the Great Commission – Go and make disciples! The Great Commission has four instructions. Read the text below and Do exercise 1. Find the four verbs in The Great Commission.
“The Great Commission” is Jesus’ final instructions to the disciples. Read about it and answer the questions below:

All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Therefore, go and make disciples of all nations, and baptize them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teach them to obey everything I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, to the very end of age.
Matthew 28.18-20
What are the four instructions Jesus gives to his disciples?
Go
Make
Baptize
Teach
And the answers are:
The four verbs in the Great Commission are a) Go, b) Make, c) Baptize, and d) Teach.
Now let’s do Exercise 2. It’s a Grammar Exercise. Look at the underlined words:
a. Given to me; Jesus
b. And baptize them;
c. teach them,
d. I have commanded you,
e. I am with you.
Read the text again and say what do the words refer to? For example: All authority has been given to me. The word “me” refers to Jesus.
And the answers are:
The new disciples
The new disciples
Jesus’s disciples
Jesus’s disciples
Essas palavras sublinhadas são pronomes, ou seja, palavras que você usa para não repetir os nomes. Olha como esse texto ficaria estranho e repetitivo se não fossem os pronomes:
Go and make disciples of all nations. Baptize the new disciples and teach the new disciples all that I have commanded my disciples. I am with my disciples until the very end of age.
Perceberam como fica estranho? Para isso servem os pronomes.
Nas Lessons 1 a 4, aprendemos os pronomes que ficam antes dos verbos, no lugar do sujeito na oração, ou seja, “subject pronouns”.
I am Jesus.
He is from Brazil.
We are fine.
They are not here.
Em português, esses pronomes são chamados de pronomes do caso reto.
Já os pronomes do Exercício 2 que acabamos de fazer, note que ficam após os verbos ou preposições:
All authority has been given to me
Preposição + pronoun
to + me
Verb + pronoun
Baptize them.
Esse tipo de pronome em inglês é chamado de “object pronoun”, pois fica no lugar do objeto, ou seja, o complemento do verbo.
Em português, esse tipo de pronome é chamado de pronome do caso oblíquo.
Resumindo:
Subject Pronouns (before verbs)
I am with you always.
They listen to Jesus.
Object Pronouns (after verbs or prepositions)
All authority has been given to me.
Baptize them.
These are the object pronouns in English. It is very simple – one subject pronoun – one object pronoun
Listen to the song, “Go!” It’s a song about the Great Commission. Listen and complete with the SUBJECT or OBJECT pronouns.
